clue.text: No gods in his gallery

parts.note: a ...' gallery is a police collection of photographs of criminals, not of deities, so the clue asks who does hang in it

explanation.surface: A remark about an art collector who hangs no images of deities.
explanation.walkthrough: A rogues' gallery is the police file of mugshots of known criminals; 'gallery' looks like art but points to that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The person pictured in a rogues' gallery is a criminal or scoundrel.

clue.text: Grain journal recommended for word-eaters

parts.note: rice is a grain
a journal is a newspaper, a paper

explanation.surface: A cereal magazine endorsed for people who devour words.
explanation.walkthrough: People who 'eat their words' must take back what they said; this thin paper is edible.
explanation.definitionFit: Edible sheets made from grain are suitable for someone forced to eat what they wrote.

clue.text: Faux pas put the 'old man right off

indicators.note: off means taken away, so the letter for right is removed from the word

parts.note: gaffer is slang for an old man or boss

explanation.surface: A social blunder that put the old fellow right off.
explanation.walkthrough: GAFFER, a British word for an old man or the boss, loses R. 'put the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A social blunder is a tactless slip.

clue.text: The next real change comes from outside

indicators.note: change means alter, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A claim that the next genuine reform will come from outsiders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges NEXT and REAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Exterior or outer is what the adjective means.

clue.text: Exploring down under, making work for tinkers ?

explanation.surface: Someone exploring Australia while drumming up trade for travelling menders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' sounds like Australia but means underground caves; tinkers were travelling menders of pots and pans, so putting holes in pots gives them work.
explanation.definitionFit: Caving underground is the sport, and punching holes in metal pans would make repair jobs for itinerant menders.

clue.text: The lane with no double yellow line ?

definitions.text: The lane with no double yellow line

parts.words: The lane with no double yellow line
parts.note: double yellow lines in Britain ban ..., so a street without them is one where you may leave a car, here the London street

explanation.surface: A question about a road free of parking restrictions.
explanation.walkthrough: Double yellow lines in Britain mean no parking; Park Lane is a famous London street, so 'the lane' where you can park.
explanation.definitionFit: Park Lane is a road in Mayfair, London, and leaving a car somewhere is to do this.

clue.text: Spring mattress for tossing and turning ?

definitions.text: Spring mattress for tossing and turning

parts.words: Spring mattress for tossing and turning
parts.note: tossing and turning sounds like insomnia in bed, but means somersaults on a springy gymnastic mat

explanation.surface: A bed for a restless sleeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossing and turning' suggests a sleepless night; here it is gymnasts flipping on a sprung canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprung canvas frame for bouncing and somersaulting fits a springy mat for flips.

clue.text: Foil — not in one of five senses

parts.note: out is the opposite of in
the five wits was an old phrase for the five senses, so one of them is a wit

explanation.surface: A fencing weapon described as lacking one of the human senses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foil' suggests fencing but means thwart; Shakespearean English spoke of 'five wits', the senses.
explanation.definitionFit: To thwart someone is to get the better of them by cleverness.

clue.text: Hop a ridge madly — that's in character

indicators.note: madly suggests wild disorder, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone jumping wildly over a hilltop, which is in their nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges HOP A RIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A written symbol standing for an idea, like a Chinese character, is such a sign.

clue.text: This work is uninformed

parts.note: the compound 'this-work' names labour done without knowledge, the kind of estimating done blind

explanation.surface: A critic dismissing a piece of writing as ignorant.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer before 'work' to get a compound meaning estimates made without facts.
explanation.definitionFit: An estimate made without knowledge is a conjecture.

clue.text: Smiles would go along with service here

definitions.text: Smiles would go along with service here

parts.words: Smiles would go along with service here
parts.note: plays on the phrase 'service with a smile' and the self-service eatery where diners serve themselves

explanation.surface: A remark about friendly staff in a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: In a self-service eatery diners serve themselves, so any 'service with a smile' is the customer's own grin.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-service restaurant is where customers carry their own trays along the counter.

clue.text: Subject the Middle English

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A student naming the topic of study: medieval English.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic or subject of a talk or essay is its main idea.

clue.text: The craft of a linesman ?

parts.note: a linesman sounds like a football official or telegraph worker, but here is someone who writes lines of verse

explanation.surface: A question about what a football assistant referee's job involves.
explanation.walkthrough: A linesman is an official at a football match, or a worker on telephone lines; here he writes lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse-making is the art of someone who composes metrical lines.

clue.text: Hamlet's woodcock-catching vows

parts.note: in Hamlet Polonius dismisses the prince's vows of love to Ophelia as snares set to catch woodcocks, gullible birds

explanation.surface: A reference to promises made by Shakespeare's prince.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius tells Ophelia that Hamlet's vows are 'springes to catch woodcocks': snares for foolish birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old term for snares or traps for birds, as Polonius uses it of the prince's promises.

clue.text: Girl's put out in round of engagement breaking

parts.note: Di is a short girl's name, here with its possessive

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the ring

parts.note: an engagement ring is a round band

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters of put are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman upset during an engagement that is falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' jumbles the letters of 'put' and 'in' sets them within the ring; 'breaking' looks like part of the engagement story but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Interrupting or disturbing something is breaking it up.

clue.text: Coil placed to correct a minor fault

indicators.note: to correct something is to set it right by rearranging, so the letters of the two words are reordered

explanation.surface: Instructions for fixing a small electrical problem by repositioning a coil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to correct' rearranges COIL and PLACED into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A peccadillo is a small sin or trivial offence.

clue.text: Job's no help. May keep baby quiet

explanation.surface: Two remarks: one about Job's useless friends, one about soothing an infant.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'Job's comforter' makes things worse, like Job's friends in the Bible; in Britain a baby's dummy, or pacifier, is also called this.
explanation.definitionFit: Job's friends who only added to his misery, and a rubber teat for an infant, share the same name.

clue.text: Not a thing to turn for keeping cool

definitions.text: Not a thing to turn for keeping cool

parts.words: Not a thing to turn for keeping cool
parts.note: recalls the idiom 'not turn a ...', meaning to show no sign of alarm, so the thing one keeps still is the clue's subject

explanation.surface: Advice that some dial should not be turned to keep a room cool.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'not turn a hair' is to stay perfectly calm; 'turn' sounds like adjusting a thermostat.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying unruffled is described by the idiom about not stirring a single strand on the head.

clue.text: Where our man in India lived in state

definitions.text: Where our man in India lived in state

parts.words: Where our man in India lived in state
parts.note: in British India an official called the Resident represented the crown at a princely court, and his official home had a name

explanation.surface: A description of a British envoy's grand home in India.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Resident at an Indian princely court lived in an official house of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Resident's official home in a princely state was so called.

clue.text: 2 sounds the larger type of this

definitions.text: 2 sounds the larger type of this

parts.words: 2 sounds the larger type of this
parts.note: the answer to 2 down sounds like gaff, a large hooked tool for landing big catches

explanation.surface: A claim that number two names the big version of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 down is GAFFE, which sounds like gaff: a large barbed hook for landing big fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaff is a big hook on a pole, a larger kind of angler's barb.

clue.text: Capital presumably not produced by the night shift either

definitions.text: Capital presumably not produced by the night shift either

parts.words: Capital presumably not produced by the night shift either
parts.note: extends the proverb that a certain capital was not built in a day: if not by the day shift, not by the night shift either

explanation.surface: A grumble that some factory output did not come from night workers.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says this city 'wasn't built in a day'; the clue adds that the night shift didn't build it either.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian capital is the city of the proverb about patient building.

clue.text: Waves to husky beauties ?

explanation.surface: Someone greeting attractive people with hoarse voices.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it gives BRAN DISHES: bran is cereal husks, and 'dishes' is slang for attractive people.
explanation.definitionFit: Flourishing a sword is waving it about; dishes of husk cereal are dishes of bran.

clue.text: Result of Longfellow's arrow feat

explanation.surface: The outcome of a poet's archery achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's poem begins 'I shot an arrow into the air', so his feat was shooting up.
explanation.definitionFit: The outcome of something, and an arrow fired skywards, share these letters.

clue.text: Perhaps a deadly way to ensure cleaner smoking

definitions.text: Perhaps a deadly way to ensure cleaner smoking

parts.words: Perhaps a deadly way to ensure cleaner smoking
parts.note: one reading is a hunter's dart weapon, the other is clearing a tobacco bowl and stem by puffing through them

explanation.surface: A grim suggestion about making smoking less dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the hunting tube that fires darts, deadly perhaps; the other is blowing through a tobacco pipe to clear it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tube for shooting poisoned darts can kill, and puffing air through a smoker's bowl clears it.

clue.text: Adds polish to the regiment

explanation.surface: Someone shining the uniforms of a regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Buffs was a famous British infantry regiment, the Royal East Kent Regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: To shine something is to rub it up, and the Royal East Kent Regiment had this nickname from its coat facings.

clue.text: Chucked about fifty as a protection

indicators.note: about means surrounding here, so the word for chucked goes round the letter for fifty

parts.note: to shy is to throw, so chucked is shied
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone throwing roughly fifty things to defend themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A buckler held up to ward off blows is a protective device.

clue.text: Ahasuerus's queen is heard in the compound

indicators.note: is heard means the name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: in the Bible Esther was queen to King Ahasuerus

explanation.surface: A Persian king's queen appears within some chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: Esther, Ahasuerus's queen in the Bible, sounds like this chemistry word.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical substance formed from an acid and an alcohol is an organic compound.

clue.text: Obstructive political association ?

parts.note: an alliance of nations acting together sounds like a barrier that obstructs

explanation.surface: A question about a party that blocks legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a group of allied countries sounds like 'block', something that obstructs.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of nations allied for common action is such an association.

clue.text: Go to buffet, choose portion to bring back

indicators.note: a portion is a part, so only part of the words buffet choose is taken, the run spanning the two

explanation.surface: Instructions to go to a buffet, select a helping and carry it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'portion' takes letters straddling 'buffET CHoose'.
explanation.definitionFit: To go and get something and return with it is to retrieve it.

clue.text: I will shortly have acquired full marks, by bad means

parts.note: I'll is the short form of I will
have acquired means got
ten out of ten is full marks

explanation.surface: A student boasting of a perfect score achieved by cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' signals the contraction I'LL; full marks are taken as a score of ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obtained dishonestly or unfairly was gained by bad means.

clue.text: Eccentric categorist loses nothing of value in' campaign

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the remaining letters are jumbled
loses means one letter is dropped from the word categorist

parts.note: O is nought, nothing

explanation.surface: An odd classifier misses something valuable during a campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' drops O from CATEGORIST, leaving CATEGRIST, which 'Eccentric' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Something important in planning a military operation is described as of tactical or overall planning value.

clue.text: A bit of Ireland seems to' stray, into Kentucky

indicators.note: into puts the word for stray inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: KY is the US postal abbreviation for Kentucky
to err is to stray

explanation.surface: Part of Ireland seems to have wandered off into an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: An Irish county; 'seems to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A county in south-west Ireland is a part of the country.
